description:
We are a team of friends interested in technology and environmental challenges. We are looking for someone who knows about forest fire behavior, wildfires, or Earth science and can help us better understand the scientific side of the project.

If you have at least one of these skills, we would be happy to have you join us!
summary:
When a satellite map shows a spike in hotspots, how can you tell whether it’s unusual for that place and season?

We’re Team QUANTUM UNKNOWNS, and we built AMBER EYE to answer that question. A newer sensor can pick up smaller hotspots, so we put more than 20 years of NASA FIRMS observations from MODIS and VIIRS on a common scale. In tests across Peru, weighted monthly accuracy scores reached 89.8% for MODIS and 94.3% for NOAA-20, both calibrated to VIIRS Suomi NPP.

That common scale lets the calendar flag unusual months. The map then shows where hotspots cluster and whether they’re near settlements or protected areas. Teams can share detection records with their source and confidence and consult an assistant that cites the evidence behind its answers. Monthly forecasts include uncertainty ranges where the model met our evaluation criteria.

In Madre de Dios, Peru, for example, AMBER EYE showed nearly two-thirds more satellite-detected thermal activity in September 2024 than in a typical September.

When a region sees a spike like that, AMBER EYE helps teams decide where to look first, giving them a chance to "Stop the spark before it leaves a mark".
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

When a region sees a spike in satellite hotspots, its own history helps tell whether that activity is unusual. We’re Team QUANTUM UNKNOWNS, and we built AMBER EYE to make that comparison possible.

The historical calendar covers 2000 to the present for areas covered by NASA FIRMS archives. On the map, users can search worldwide by place or coordinates, view hotspots from the past 1, 7, 14, 21, or 30 days, and download the results as CSV.

AMBER EYE counts each equal area 1 km, 500m or 375 m grid cell once per sensor per UTC day when it contains an eligible detection. Using overlapping MODIS and VIIRS observations, we estimate a calibration factor for each region and calendar month and express the historical series on the VIIRS Suomi NPP scale. The calendar flags unusual months, shows seasonal peaks and historical ranges, and compares a month in progress with the same days in earlier years. It also labels provisional data and gaps.

2. What benefits does it have? What is the intended impact?

A land manager can see whether current activity is unusual for the season. Response teams can check which hotspots are near communities or protected areas before deciding where to investigate. Researchers can inspect the calibration factors and export the monthly series for independent review.

In September 2024, AMBER EYE calculated 2,743 cell-days of detected thermal activity in Madre de Dios, Peru. The calendar lets teams compare that figure with earlier Septembers and share the evidence behind their assessment.

We would measure impact by how quickly teams identify priority areas, how often flagged detections receive field follow-up, and whether another team can reproduce the analysis from the exports.

3. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

We built the web app with TypeScript, React, CSS, Vite, and MapLibre GL. The backend processes historical archives by country, stores reusable tiles, and serves the API. We deployed the demo on a Hostinger VPS with Docker Compose and persistent storage. Node.js and JavaScript ES modules handle data processing and forecast evaluation. The server keeps the FIRMS API key and caches recent queries.

NASA FIRMS supplies observations from MODIS on Terra and Aqua and VIIRS on Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21. Photon and Nominatim power place search. geoBoundaries, WDPA, and NASA HBASE provide administrative boundaries, protected areas, and settlement context. Nodemailer supports email subscriptions where SMTP is configured, and the evidence assistant has a local document mode and an optional LangChain and OpenAI integration.

We used Vitest, React Testing Library, jsdom, and TypeScript checks to verify the analysis, API, and interface. Git and GitHub tracked code changes, and Linear tracked requirements, owners, dependencies, and review evidence.

Github code: https://github.com/EderDavid1/Map-Nasa_GOTG

4. How is your project creative? What factors did your team consider?

We designed AMBER EYE around the questions a land manager asks when a map shows a spike. Is it unusual for this season? Where are the detections concentrated? What evidence can I share with my team? The calendar, map, and observation records answer those questions in one workflow.

Sensor sensitivity shaped the science. We used overlapping observations to calibrate each region and calendar month, and equal-area cells to limit the effect of repeated observations. Seasonality shaped the comparison, so partial months use the same elapsed days in earlier years. Data availability shaped the display, so provisional observations and gaps remain visible. Request limits shaped the architecture, so we prepare compact country archives on demand and reuse them across regional queries.

Field decisions shaped the map. Settlements, protected areas, and separately sourced reported incidents provide context for verification. Accessibility shaped the calendar, with numbers and symbols alongside color, responsive layouts, and study views in English and Spanish. Reproducibility shaped the exports, which include the method version and calibration factors. Forecasts show uncertainty where the model met evaluation criteria, and the evidence assistant cites the sources behind its explanations. Together, these choices help a team understand an unusual month and decide where to investigate first.

Our Business Model Canvas shows how we plan to bring AMBER EYE to wildfire response teams and keep it available to them over time.

And finally, meet the team that built it. Here’s what each member contributed and how the pieces of our solution work together to help responders use wildfire data to make faster, better-informed decisions.

At sunrise, there’s a thin line of smoke above the ridge. By nightfall, that fire could force families from their homes. We built AMBER EYE to help crews decide where to act while there’s still a chance to keep the fire small.

So remember: "Stop the spark before it leaves a mark".
